n: In this lecture we make an introduction to forensic medicine. Forensic medicine is an independent medical science. It serves to resolve medico-biological questions needed by the courts, investigative bodies and bodies of inquiry. Outline of the lecture: concepts of the science and of examination, subject, links with other sciences, principles, objects, history, types and documents. Its importance for the paediatrician is that if there is no document on age, or a document raises doubt, an examination is ordered to establish the person's age. As a result the student distinguishes the expert from the specialist, lists the types of examination and knows the parts of the expert's conclusion.

The concept of forensic medicine. Forensic medicine is an independent medical science; it studies the medico-biological questions arising in the activity of the courts, investigative bodies and bodies of inquiry. Science is the body of scientific knowledge on establishing, investigating and assessing medical facts and circumstances that become a source of evidence for law enforcement bodies. Forensic medical examination is the practical application of this knowledge. It resolves the task set by the court, investigation or inquiry, and ends with the expert's conclusion. Attention, there is a risk of error: forensic medicine is a body of scientific knowledge, whereas forensic medical examination is an investigation carried out in a definite order. These two concepts are not the same.

Four features of examination. In essence, examination is an investigation, and it has four features. The first is the specialist: the investigation is carried out by a specialist with the knowledge and skills of the field. The second is a specific task: the investigation is carried out on a specific task, usually for the purpose of assessment. The third is a strict procedure, that is, the procedure is strictly determined. The fourth is the document: the process and results are formalised in a corresponding document. These four features distinguish examination from an ordinary investigation.

The process of forensic medical examination. Forensic medical examination is an investigation resolving the task set by the court, investigation and inquiry. The process consists of four stages. At the first stage the body sets the task. At the second, the investigation is carried out with medical knowledge. At the third, the established procedure is observed. At the fourth, the expert's conclusion is drawn up. The four features of examination: a specialist carries it out, there is a specific task, the procedure is strict, it is formalised in a document. Remember: forensic medicine is the science, forensic medical examination its practical application.

The subject of forensic medicine. The subject of forensic medicine is the theory and practice of forensic medical examination. For the first time, in 1948, M. I. Avdeev proposed a scientifically grounded system of the subject of the science. This system is connected with the objects of examination. The system consists of eight directions. The first directions: history of the science, organisational and procedural questions, impairment of health and death under external factors, examination of the body. The remaining directions: examination of living persons, of physical evidence, of materials of investigation and court, and of professional offences of medical workers.

t: Modern constituent parts of the science
n: Modern constituent parts of the science. At present, by content, the science consists of nine constituent parts. The first group is the foundations: history, and organisational and procedural foundations. The second is death and injury: thanatology and traumatology. The third is special fields: obstetrics-gynaecology and toxicology. The fourth is evidence and factors: biology, external factors and identification. V. L. Popov in 1999 distinguished mainly three doctrines: of death, of injuries and of identification of a person. In 2002 "Professional offences of medical workers" separated out as an independent science.

t: Popov's doctrines and separation of a science
n: Popov's doctrines and separation of a science. V. L. Popov in 1999, by the content of the science, distinguishes three doctrines: of death and postmortem changes, of injuries, of identification of a person. The present nine parts are as follows: history, organisational-procedural foundations, thanatology, traumatology, obstetrics-gynaecology, toxicology, biology, external factors and identification. In 2002 the section "Professional offences of medical workers" separated out and became an independent science, "Legal foundations of the doctor's activity". Attention: Popov's three doctrines and the present nine constituent parts are not the same. The first are the main directions of the science, the second its full content.

t: Case analysis: concepts of science and examination
n: Now a case analysis. Situation: the investigator issued a ruling and asked for the cause of death to be established on a body. A specialist carried out the investigation and drew up the expert's conclusion. Analysis: this is forensic medical examination. Its four features: a specialist carries it out, there is a specific task, the procedure is strict, the result is formalised in a document. Forensic medicine, however, is the science: it studies the theory and practice of examination. Examination is the practical application of the knowledge of this science. Think: which of the four features of examination are met in this situation? Why would an investigation without the investigator's instruction not be an examination?

t: Links of forensic medicine with other sciences
n: Links of forensic medicine with other sciences. Forensic medicine is not a fundamental but an applied science; it is connected with medical, legal, natural and philosophical sciences. The fundamental medical sciences are the foundation, and without mastering them no examination can be carried out. Of the clinical sciences, traumatology, obstetrics and ophthalmology are needed. Chemistry is needed in the investigation of poisons, and physics in assessing the effect of temperature and electric current. Philosophy and logic are applied in dialectical assessment and in drawing up conclusions. Attention: the treating doctor is not an expert. One approaches for the sake of treatment, the other for legal assessment.

t: Approach of the expert and the treating doctor
n: The approach of the expert and the treating doctor. The clinical specialist attends to diagnosis and treatment, and the expert to legal assessment of the state. The aim of the treating doctor is treatment and prevention. The aim of the forensic medical expert is legal assessment. The expert uses clinical knowledge: in injury, knowledge of traumatology is needed, in criminal abortion gynaecology, in eye injury ophthalmology. Attention: it is impossible to know fully all specialties of medicine; the expert's aim is legal assessment.

Principles of examination. The Law of the Republic of Uzbekistan "On Forensic Examination" recognises five basic principles. These are legality, observance of human rights, independence of the expert, objectivity, and comprehensiveness and completeness. These principles were generalised by studying and analysing many years of expert practice. The expert's investigations must always be scientifically grounded.

t: Independence, responsibility and the period of identification
n: Independence, responsibility and the period of identification. Attention: independence does not mean irresponsibility. Procedural independence gives rise to personal responsibility for the investigation, result and conclusion. The expert may act only within his competence. The right of initiative is recorded in the relevant laws. Initiative means that the expert, besides the questions put, may express an opinion on other questions that relate to the subject of the examination and are important for the case. Another aspect: objects are a source of evidence only during a certain period. Abrasions and bruises are mostly examined up to 10-15 days, and the body as soon as possible.

Quick questions on concepts and principles. First question: the four features of an expert investigation? A specialist carries it out, on a specific task, in a strict procedure, and the result is formalised in a document. Second question: what is the subject of forensic medicine? The theory and practice of forensic medical examination; its scientific system was proposed in 1948 by M. I. Avdeev. Third question: the main principles recognised by law? Legality, observance of human rights, independence of the expert, objectivity, comprehensiveness and completeness. Attention, risk of error! The treating doctor directs his approach to diagnosis and treatment, the forensic medical expert to legal assessment of the state.

Objects and methods of examination. Objects: the body, living persons, physical evidence, materials of criminal and civil cases. Objects are submitted by the person who ordered the examination, who answers for their authenticity. Methods are divided into three groups. General scientific methods include observation, description, measurement and comparison. Particular methods: morphological, radiological and chemical. Special methods: photo comparison and comparative study. In practice only methods permitted or recommended by the Chief Forensic Medical Examination are used.

t: Case analysis: choice of object and method
n: Case analysis on choice of object and method. Situation: a knife was found at the scene, and there is an injury on the victim's skin. Which group of methods is applied? A special method. The properties of the skin injury and of the knife are studied comparatively, and the injuring weapon is determined. The knife is examined as physical evidence, and the injury as an object of a living person or a body. For discussion: the chosen method must allow repeated checking, and the results must be documented.

t: History: from the ancient world to the Middle Ages
n: History: from the ancient world to the Middle Ages. The laws of Lycurgus date from the 9th–8th century BC; rules for examination of the body were added to the laws of Sparta, and Hippocrates also took part in preparing them. The body of Julius Caesar in 44 BC was examined by the physician Antistius: of 23 wounds only one led to death. The Code of Justinian dates from the 6th century. In it the participation of doctors and midwives is obligatory, and their conclusion is placed above the testimony of witnesses. "Xi Yuan Lu" dates from 1247.

History: 13th-19th centuries in Europe. The stages of development are in sequence: 13th–14th centuries Lucca and surgeons, 1532 the Carolina law, 16th century the work of Paré, 1681 Schreyer's lung test, then the name "forensic medicine" proposed by Bohn. In 1532 the Carolina made the participation of a doctor obligatory in cases of homicide, poisoning, miscarriage and the like. Paré's work covers injuries, carbon monoxide and lightning strike and gives models of forensic medical conclusions. In the 19th century scientists such as Virchow, Rokitansky, Hofmann, Brouardel and Orfila made a significant contribution to the science.

t: Pirogov, the 20th century and scientists of Central Asia
n: Pirogov, the 20th century and scientists of Central Asia. Pirogov in his atlas of 1846 described examination of the body; in the Caucasus report and works on military field surgery he gave information on gunshot injuries. In the 20th century, especially after the Second World War, research accelerated and many textbooks and manuals were created. In the works of Biruni, Ibn Sina and Jurjani there is information relating to forensic medicine; in sharia-based justice, however, the doctor was not involved. Attention: the information in Ibn Sina's "Canon of Medicine" on postmortem changes, poisons and injuries was written for correct medical care.

History of departments in Uzbekistan. The first department was organised in 1920 in the medical faculty of Turkestan University. Then departments were opened in Samarkand in 1935, in Andijan in 1959 and in the Tashkent Paediatric Medical Institute in 1972. In 1993 a forensic medicine course was opened at the Tashkent Institute for Advanced Training of Doctors. That is, the science in Uzbekistan developed gradually through departments.

Case analysis on evaluating historical information. Situation: Ibn Sina's "Canon of Medicine" contains information on postmortem changes, kinds of violent death, poisons and injuries. This information was written not for the administration of justice but mainly for giving correct medical care in such cases. Attention, there is a risk of error: the presence of information relating to forensic medicine does not mean the presence of forensic medical examination. Until the beginning of the 20th century representatives of medicine were not summoned to court. Question: can we call Ibn Sina's work the beginning of the science of forensic medicine? Justify your answer with the purpose stated in the book.

Quick questions on history. First question: who examined the body of Julius Caesar and how many of the 23 wounds were assessed as leading to death? Second question: with which state or ruler are "Xi Yuan Lu", "Carolina" and the "Code of Justinian" connected? Match them. Third question: which test did I. Schreyer first apply in 1681 in examining the body of a newborn? Fourth question: in what year was the department of forensic medicine organised at the Tashkent Paediatric Medical Institute? Check the answers yourself from the previous slides.

t: Four periods of the service in Uzbekistan
n: Four periods of the service in Uzbekistan. In the formation of the forensic medical expert service of Uzbekistan, four periods are conventionally distinguished. Period I up to the 1920s: episodic examinations. Period II up to the 1950s: on the basis of departments, with a cabinet opened in 1945. Period III 1950–1991: the Chief Bureau and territorial bureaux. Period IV from 1991: an independent service and a new law. In period I there was no expert institution in Turkestan, and official examinations were carried out only episodically. Attention: the cabinet of 1945 belongs to period II, the Chief Bureau of 1950 to period III.

t: Early periods and the period of independence
n: Early periods and the period of independence. Under the forensic medicine statute of 1842, in the first instance hospital doctors carried out the examination at the request of administrative bodies. In complex cases the second instance took part, that is, heads of hospitals and district doctors. The third, highest instance, the medical council, gave the final conclusion. In period II the examination was carried out in departments of medical higher education institutions by professors and teachers; forensic medical laboratories were opened at departments. In the period of independence the Law of the Republic of Uzbekistan "On Forensic Examination" was adopted for the first time and new normative documents were developed.

Legal terms. Forensic medical examinations are most often ordered in criminal investigation, so they are connected with the Criminal Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure, that is, the CCP. The CCP determines the procedure for investigating a criminal case, trying it in court, and the relations of participants. Law is obligatory rules guaranteed by the state. A statute is a generally binding normative act. A code is a systematised collection of statutes. The Criminal Code defines crimes and measures of punishment. Attention: the Criminal Code determines what is a crime, and the CCP how the case is dealt with.

t: CCP Article 173: mandatory cases of examination
n: CCP Article 173: mandatory cases of examination. Article 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure lists the cases in which ordering and carrying out an examination is obligatory. First of all, the cause of death and the nature and degree of severity of bodily injuries are established. Signs of sexual intercourse, pregnancy and artificial termination of pregnancy are also established by examination. If there is no document or it is doubtful, the person's age is established. The physical condition and the need for treatment of an infectious disease are also checked.

t: Place of ordering and carrying out the examination
n: Place of ordering and carrying out the examination. Forensic medical examination is carried out on the ruling of the bodies of inquiry or investigation, or on a court order. Depending on the place, the examination may be carried out in the bureau, outside it or in a mixed manner. When carried out in the bureau, the conditions are provided by the head of the institution. Outside the bureau, however, providing conditions is the responsibility of the person who ordered the examination. In the mixed variant part is carried out in the bureau and part outside; as an example one may name exhumation at a cemetery and laboratory examination.

Examination in judicial investigation. Examination in the court session is entrusted to the experts who gave the conclusion in the preliminary investigation, or to others appointed by the court, or to them together. At the request of the parties or on its own initiative the court issues an order and reads it out in the session. Attention: unlike in the preliminary investigation, in judicial investigation the expert takes full part in the sessions and in checking the circumstances of the case. The expert puts questions to those being questioned and becomes acquainted with the written evidence. The written conclusion is read out in the session and appended to the record.

Forensic expert: rights and duties. The expert becomes acquainted with the case materials and files a petition requesting additional materials or objects. Under the right of initiative he expresses an opinion in the conclusion also on questions not asked but important for the case. His rights further include making a statement on a wrong interpretation. His duties are as follows: he examines the objects fully, does not independently collect materials, gives the conclusion objectively and with justification, and does not disclose information. That is, rights and duties work together.

The difference between specialist and expert. The specialist assists the investigation and court in finding and documenting a medical fact that is evidence. He takes part in inspection and examination; the basis is Article 69 of the CCP. The expert, however, establishes and assesses the medical fact, carries out the investigation and documents it in the form of a conclusion; the basis is the Law on Forensic Examination. Attention: a specialist is not an expert. The specialist does not draw up an independent document, whereas the expert gives a conclusion. A person who was a specialist in this case may later be appointed as an expert.

Challenge and criminal liability. Grounds for challenge: kinship, material, official or other dependence on interested parties, and also lack of sufficient qualification in the specialty. The expert may declare self-recusal, or interested parties may declare a challenge. Only the person who ordered the examination decides it. Time limit: in inquiry and preliminary investigation a challenge is decided within 24 hours; in the court session in that session itself, immediately. Liability under the Criminal Code: for a knowingly wrong conclusion Article 238, for unauthorised disclosure of information Article 239, for refusal to give a conclusion Article 240.

t: Case analysis: status of expert and specialist
n: Case analysis on the status of expert and specialist. Situation: the investigator summoned a doctor of a medical institution as a specialist to examine a living person. The specialist assists in finding and documenting the medical fact, but in the procedural action does not draw up an independent document. Attention: do not make the mistake. A person who was a specialist in this case may later be appointed as an expert, and this is not an obstacle. Question: what is done if the doctor is a relative of the patient? Who decides the challenge, and within what time in the preliminary investigation?

Quick questions on procedural foundations. First question: if there is no document or it raises doubt, according to Article 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, what is established about whom? Second question: does the expert in the conclusion answer only the questions put to him or can he express an opinion on other important questions as well? Third question: within how many hours is a challenge made in the preliminary investigation or inquiry decided, and who decides it? Fourth question: on the basis of which documents is forensic medical examination carried out? Answer each question yourself from the previous slides.

Procedural types of examination. Primary examination is carried out on a body, a living person and physical evidence, usually by one expert. Commission examination is carried out in a complex case and in professional offence by a commission of experts. In complex examination sciences other than medicine are also needed, and each expert works within his competence. Additional examination is ordered to supplement, repeat examination to check again. Repeat examination is ordered if the conclusion is unfounded or doubtful; disagreement of the parties is not in itself a ground. Entrusting repeat examination to the expert who carried out the original is forbidden. Attention: repeat, commission and complex examinations are carried out only in the repeat, commission department of the bureau.

The difference between additional and repeat examination. Attention: additional examination is not repeat examination. Their aim, reason for ordering and performer differ. Additional examination is ordered to fill a shortcoming and gap, is usually carried out by the former expert, and considers a newly identified question. Repeat examination rechecks a doubtful conclusion; here not the former expert but two or more experts work, and the former questions are put again. Disagreement of the parties with the former conclusion cannot in itself be a ground for ordering repeat examination. The ruling for repeat examination must state the reasons for disagreeing with the former conclusion.

The expert conclusion and other documents. The expert conclusion is considered in an order of four parts: introductory, with date, ground and questions; investigation, with methods and results; finding, that is, answers to the questions; and evaluation, in which investigation and court evaluate the conclusion. The expert conclusion has no obligatory evidential force in advance; it is evaluated along with other evidence. If the investigator or court does not agree with the conclusion, they must justify this in the ruling or order. In the act, however, no receipt on liability is taken, and its final part is called the "conclusion".

t: Structure of the service in Uzbekistan
n: Structure of the service in Uzbekistan. The system: the Chief Bureau, 13 territorial bureaux and their district, inter-district and city units. A territorial bureau is subordinate in administrative and financial matters to the health authority, and in examination to the Chief Bureau. The morphological department carries out examination of bodies and microscopy. The forensic medical outpatient clinic examines living persons. The forensic chemical department deals with toxicology, the forensic biological department with blood, hair and stains. The repeat and commission department carries out repeat, commission and complex examination. The department of medical criminalistics examines the mechanism of injury, weapons and identification of a person.

t: Case analysis: choice of type of examination
n: Case analysis on choice of the type of examination. First situation: in a complex road traffic accident a child was injured. The injury is determined by medical knowledge, and the circumstances of the accident by automotive-technical knowledge. Which examination is ordered? If a science other than medicine is needed, a complex examination is carried out, and each expert answers his own part. Second situation: the former expert's conclusion is unfounded or there is doubt about its correctness. Which examination is ordered, and who does not carry it out? Attention: disagreement of the parties with the conclusion is not a ground for repeat examination. The ruling states the reasons for disagreeing with the original conclusion.

Let us summarise. Forensic medicine studies medico-biological questions for the court, investigation and inquiry. Its knowledge is applied in practice in the form of forensic medical examination. Types of examination: primary, commission, complex, additional and repeat. The expert conclusion is one item of evidence and in advance has no evidential force. For the paediatrician: a doctor of a medical institution may be involved as a specialist, more often in examination of a living person; the specialist does not draw up an independent document. Questions for independent work: how do expert and specialist differ? How do commission and complex examination differ? When is a challenge decided?
